claim: BIG Launcher replaces the Android home screen with a grid of oversized buttons; its pitch is single-touch operation with no gestures: no swipes, no long-press menus.
quote: No swipe gestures. No long-press menus. One touch takes them where they want to go. They always know where they are.
notes: Vendor-authored.

claim: BIG Launcher's SOS flow: one tap on a red SOS button sends an SMS with GPS location to pre-set family contacts and calls a designated person on speakerphone, with a short countdown to cancel accidental taps.
quote: One tap on the red SOS button sends an SMS with their location to the family members you chose and calls you on speakerphone. A short countdown lets them cancel an accidental tap.
notes: SOS = SMS-location + speakerphone call + cancel countdown; borrowable pattern.

claim: BIG Launcher uses a caregiver-setup model: a family member configures the home screen, hides unused apps, and locks settings behind a password so the senior cannot break the configuration.
quote: You configure everything, then lock the settings with a password. Your parent uses the phone freely without undoing your setup.
notes: Caregiver-admin / password-lock is the dominant pattern across competitors.

claim: BIG Launcher puts contacts on the home screen as large photo buttons - marketed specifically for dementia users who may forget names.
quote: Photo contacts mean they tap a face - not a name they might forget.
notes: Quote rendered with em-dash on page: 'tap a face — not a name'. Photo-dial is a recurring senior-UX pattern.

claim: BIG Launcher is monetized as a suite: launcher + separate BIG Phone, BIG SMS, BIG Alarm, BIG Notifications, BIG Remote Help apps; each free to try, paid via monthly/yearly/lifetime plans or an all-suite PREMIUM bundle; pricing varies by country.
quote: Choose a monthly, yearly or lifetime plan for one app—or unlock all four plus remote help with BIG Apps Suite PREMIUM.
notes: Modular suite partly forced by Google Play policy (separate phone/SMS apps).

claim: BIG Remote Help offers remote assistance: the senior initiates a one-tap video call, the helper sees their screen and can tap for them with permission; pairing via QR code in person; free tier is 15 minutes/month.
quote: With BIG Remote Help, they call you with one tap. You see their screen and show them where to tap—or, with their permission, tap for them.
notes: Remote-assist is a differentiator competitors are converging on (cf. Rafiqa).

claim: Vendor-acknowledged limits: BIG SMS sends text only (no photo sending), the DTMF keypad is a paid feature in BIG Phone, and the product is Android-only.
quote: BIG SMS shows photos and videos people send, but sends text only — for sharing photos, add WhatsApp to the home screen
notes: From vendor's own 'worth knowing' FAQ.

claim: BIG Launcher positions against OS simple modes: 'Easy Mode just makes Samsung's own home screen a bit bigger' while BIG adds photo contacts, SOS, hidden apps and locked settings on any Android.
quote: Easy Mode just makes Samsung's own home screen a bit bigger. BIG Launcher is built for seniors from the ground up — photo contacts, an SOS button, hidden apps, locked settings and simple apps for calls and messages — and it runs on almost any Android, not just Samsung.
notes: Useful framing for GranPhone vs EMUI/OEM easy modes.

claim: Grand Launcher (CUPLESOFT) home screen exposes 6 large functions; tapping status icons (battery, signal, date) shows an explanatory message; lists in calls/contacts show ONE item per screen with a Next button.
quote: La pantalla principal permite acceder a 6 funcionalidades diferentes... las listas presentan un elemento cada vez y tienen el botón 'próximo' para ver el siguiente elemento
notes: One-item-per-screen paging is an extreme low-cognitive-load pattern.

claim: Grand Launcher is a one-time purchase (~EUR 11.99), requires Android 6.0+, and needs separate companion apps Grand Phone and Grand SMS for calling and messaging.
quote: Tiene un precio de 11.99 euros. Es de pago único con acceso sin límite.
notes: Complaint noted: phone, messages and voice assistant require separate app downloads.

claim: Grand Launcher's advertised feature set: editable main-menu buttons, contact shortcuts on the home screen, alphabetical-order keyboard, own photo gallery/camera, password-protected options, voice assistant for the blind, color/language editors, SOS mode, silent mode, flashlight.
quote: Keyboard with letters in alphabetical order ... Password for application options and other system functions ... Voice assistant for the blind ... SOS mode, silent mode
notes: Vendor site fetched over http (broken https cert).

claim: Grand Launcher ships its own screen reader ('voz', downloadable plugin) because TalkBack worked poorly with it - and the reviewer found the plugin more intuitive than TalkBack.
quote: la aplicación no ha funcionado bien con el Talkback. En su lugar, ofrece una opción de 'voz' que hace de lector de pantalla... funciona de una manera mucho más intuitiva que el Talkback
notes: Relevant to GranPhone accessibility strategy; BaldPhone also has a voice assistant.

claim: Orientatech's complaints about Grand Launcher: the Android notification bar stays active and can confuse the user, no in-app brightness control, and the Options tree can be too deep (mitigated by password protection).
quote: la barra de notificaciones sigue activa. Esto puede confundir a la persona usuaria... en la sección de 'Opciones', este árbol puede resultar muy profundo
notes: Recurring complaint class: the stock OS keeps leaking through every senior launcher.

claim: Grand Launcher's alphabetical-order keyboard is of unproven benefit - one reviewer struggled with it and noted uncertainty whether it helps the elderly.
quote: it has a keyboard with alphabetical letters. I honestly struggle using it, but we don't know if its easier for the elderly.
notes: BaldPhone/GranPhone also ship custom keyboards; worth validating.

claim: 'Senior Launcher - Simple Phone' (Vaibhav Lakhera): oversized-icon grid, pinned favorite apps/contacts, quick actions (SOS, torch, Wi-Fi, ring modes), web shortcuts, lockable settings+home screen, adjustable grid/icon/text size, light/dark themes, third-party calling (WhatsApp/Telegram), widgets, reminders; 4.5 stars, ~1K reviews, 100K+ downloads; free trial then one-time premium.
quote: Lock settings and home screen to allow only the favourite contacts and apps — Change home grid size, icon size and text size — Light and dark theme
notes: Vendor-authored listing; actively maintained (updated Nov 2026).

claim: A Senior Launcher user complaint: it cannot block the OS pull-down settings shade, so seniors can still make inadvertent system changes - the reviewer abandoned it for that reason.
quote: with the operating system preventing the main "pull down" settings being accessed, I will not be able to prevent my elder-folk from making inadvertent changes to the system settings. For this reason, I can't go ahead.
notes: Concrete evidence that locking down notification shade/quick settings is a real user need GranPhone could solve.

claim: Senior Launcher positions privacy as a feature: no ads, no accounts, all data on-device; optional Accessibility permission used only for a Lock Screen quick action.
quote: All your data (apps, contacts) stays on your device. No ads and no accounts required.
notes: Privacy/no-account is a selling point caregivers respond to.

claim: BaldPhone is a free, open-source (Apache-2.0) full-interface replacement: home launcher, keyboard, video tutorials, pill reminders, contacts+phone apps, voice assistant, alarms, photo/video viewer, notification management, SOS button, advanced settings; requires Android 5.0+.
quote: Home Launcher — Keyboard — Video Tutorials — Reminders For Pills — Contacts and Phone Applications — Voice Assistant — Alarms — Photos and Videos Viewer — Notification Management — SOS Button — Advanced Settings
notes: GranPhone is forked from this codebase (v14.0.0 vs upstream 13.0.0).

claim: BaldPhone is distributed via F-Droid (full version), a beta APK repo, and a Google Play 'Second Version' that lacks the Recent Calls feature; upstream development stalled around Oct 2020 (v13.0.0), ~185 open issues.
quote: Note: Google Play version does not contain the Recent Calls feature.
notes: Play-policy constraints (call-log/SMS permissions) shaped the feature set - same constraint applies to GranPhone.

claim: BaldPhone requires an unusually broad permission surface: call phone numbers directly, read/write contacts and call log, modify system settings, draw over other apps, disable screen lock, run at startup, request package deletion.
quote: directly call phone numbers ... modify system settings ... This app can appear on top of other apps ... disable your screen lock
notes: A full senior-replacement UI inherently needs near-total device control; permission UX is part of setup.

claim: F-Droid flags a BaldPhone anti-feature: ACRA crash reports sent silently without consent (opt-out possible).
notes: Anti-Features section was in the indexed page but not in the fetched render; verify before relying on it.

claim: Doro's patented 'EVA' interface is action-based rather than app-based: home screen shows verb icons Call, View, Send, Add, Search, Set; 'View' opens a submenu (my messages, my call history, my pictures, etc.) - the user picks an intention, the phone picks the app.
quote: On the Home screen, Eva organises your most commonly used functions under a few, action-based icons: Call, View, Send, Add, Search and Set.
notes: Distinct IA vs icon-grid launchers; strong borrow candidate for never-used-a-phone users.

claim: Doro phones run a step-by-step first-boot guide that sets up hearing/vision/text-size settings and includes tutorials for first-time smartphone users.
quote: the Doro smartphones shows a step-by-step guide when you first turn it on. It helps you with everything from finding the best settings for your hearing and vision, to connecting with the internet and accessing your Gmail account.
notes: Onboarding-as-accessibility-setup; BaldPhone instead uses in-app video tutorials.

claim: Doro 8035: first boot asks 'Have you used a smartphone before?' and offers a beginner mode with three large bottom buttons Call/View/Send; a hardware panic button on the back texts GPS coordinates to emergency contacts via 3-second long-press or triple-press.
quote: can be set to a three-second long press, or three consecutive presses before springing into action
notes: Hardware SOS pattern; app equivalent = on-screen red button with cancel countdown (BIG Launcher).

claim: Even Doro's dedicated senior phone lets Android leak through: permission popups appear on first use of features, the notification bar is unchanged, and jargon like 'haptic feedback' slips into settings.
quote: Android can't help but poke out behind the scenes... The notifications bar, for example, is completely unchanged... you can set "the haptic feedback", which isn't a helpful term.
notes: Cross-product evidence: hiding stock-OS surfaces is the hardest, most-valued part of senior UX.

claim: Senior Safety Phone offers single-touch favorite contacts, large fonts, volume lock and layout changes in one settings place; the reviewer's only complaint was intrusive ads (removable).
quote: The only problem I noticed with this app is its advertisements. Ads can be pretty annoying for users if you don't opt to remove them.
notes: Ads in a senior app = trust/usability hazard; ad-free is a differentiator.

claim: Simple Launcher (Cloud Innovations): enlarged fonts, a single 'control center' for features, and a 'safety lock' that prevents accidental changes to volume and app positioning; includes an SOS shortcut.
quote: with its safety lock turned on, users cannot change headset volume and app positioning accidentally
notes: Volume-lock is a small, concrete feature worth borrowing (seniors often mute the phone accidentally).

claim: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires pointer-input targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (with spacing/equivalent/inline/UA/essential exceptions).
quote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels
notes: 24px is the AA floor, not the recommended level for seniors.

claim: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced, Level AAA) requires targets of at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, and WCAG itself recommends aiming for it on important controls.
quote: 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) uses the larger 44 by 44 CSS pixel measure as its threshold size
notes: Also: 'For important links/controls, consider aiming for the stricter 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced).'

claim: Small close-spaced targets disproportionately hurt users with tremors, spasticity, quadriplegia and other fine-motor limitations — the exact population of elderly users.
quote: Disabilities addressed by this requirement include hand tremors, spasticity, and quadriplegia.

claim: Android platform guidance recommends every interactive element have a touch target of at least 48x48dp, and larger is better.
quote: we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better.

claim: Material Design states 48x48dp touch target ≈ 9mm physical, and that the recommended touchscreen target size is 7-10mm; larger targets may be appropriate for a broader spectrum of users.
quote: For most platforms, consider making touch targets at least 48 x 48 dp. A touch target of this size results in a physical size of about 9mm, regardless of screen size. The recommended target size for touchscreen elements is 7-10mm. It may be appropriate to use larger touch targets to accommodate a larger spectrum of users.

claim: Material Design recommends touch targets be separated by 8dp or more of space, and iOS's recommended touch target is 44x44pt.
quote: In most cases, touch targets separated by 8dp of space or more promote balanced information density and usability.
notes: Also verbatim: 'Note that on iOS, 44 x 44 pt is the recommended touch target.'

claim: A visual element can be smaller than its touch target: e.g., a 24x24dp icon wrapped in padding to reach the full 48x48dp target.
quote: an icon may appear to be 24 x 24 dp, but the padding surrounding it comprises the full 48 x 48 dp touch target
notes: Useful for keeping a 'modern' look while keeping large hit areas.

claim: The MIT Touch Lab fingertip research (Dandekar, Raju & Srinivasan, J Biomech Eng 2003) is widely cited in touch-UI guidance as establishing the average human finger pad is 10-14mm and the average fingertip is 8-10mm.
quote: An MIT Touch Lab study of Human Fingertips to Investigate the Mechanics of Tactile Sense (PDF) found that the average human finger pad is 10-14mm and the average fingertip is 8-10mm.
notes: Primary paper verified via PMID 14618927 (eFetch); the mm figures are the attributed Touch Lab measurements circulated via this canonical secondary page and the book Mobile First.

claim: Microsoft's Windows Phone guidance recommended 9mm touch targets (7mm minimum, 2mm minimum spacing), going larger than 9mm for frequently-touched, error-severe, edge-located, or sequential-task elements like a dial pad.
quote: a recommended touch target size of 9mm/34px; a minimum touch target size of 7mm/26px; a minimum spacing between elements of 2mm/8px
notes: Quotes MS WP7 UI Design and Interaction Guide.

claim: Nokia's finger-UI minimums were 7x7mm with 1mm gaps (index finger), 8x8mm with 2mm gaps (thumb), 5mm list line spacing, and ~1cm minimum for touchable elements; a UMD one-handed-thumb study recommended ≥9.2mm (single-target) and ≥9.6mm (multi-target).
quote: 7 x 7 mm with 1 mm gaps for index finger usage
notes: Also verbatim: 'recommended target sizes at least 9.2 mm for single-target tasks and 9.6 mm for multi-target tasks.'

claim: In a controlled elderly-user study, researchers derived a minimum target size of 8mm for older adults: buttons, icons and clickable text should be at least 8mm, and much larger when targets sit close together without spacing.
quote: Use larger targets (8 mm or larger in size)... interactive objects such as buttons, icons, and clickable text should at a minimum be larger than 8 mm
notes: Kobayashi et al. 2011 INTERACT, N=20 elderly.

claim: Elderly users' tap error rates explode on small targets: 39% on 30px targets (small device) vs 6.5%/5.6% on 50px/70px; on the large device 13.6% vs 1.4%/1.7% — far above the ~4% acceptable error rate in HCI literature.
quote: For 30-pixel targets on the small device, the error rate was 39%... The error rates were 6.5% and 5.6% for 50- and 70-pixel targets, respectively, on the small device. The respective values were 13.6%, 1.4%, and 1.7% for 30-, 50-, and 70-pixel targets on the large device.
notes: Devices were large/small tablets-era screens; the mechanism (small target → errors) is the transferable finding.

claim: Elderly users tend to tap off-center to the right (systematic gap between intended and actual touch location), so visual touch feedback and forgiving target geometry matter.
quote: Address the gap between intended and actual touch locations. The elderly tend to miss their intended targets due to parallax and the large contact area of each finger.
notes: Mean x-offset +12.9px right for right-handed tapping.

claim: Counterintuitively, elderly participants found dragging and pinching easier and preferable to precise tapping — gestures are not inherently off-limits, but gesture-invoked functions must have instructions and visible clues or users never discover them.
quote: most participants in our experiment could not find those functions without guidance
notes: Full quote: 'the participants commented that dragging and pinching were preferred and easier to do than tapping... most of the participants stated that dragging was the easiest operation to perform.' Discovery is the failure mode, not the motor action.

claim: Gesture-based interfaces hide functionality: without textual labels/menus showing what is possible, elderly users stick to the few functions someone explained and get confused by functions triggered accidentally.
quote: A typical gesture-based interface on a touchscreen lacks textual labels and menus to show "what is possible with this application"... the participants tended to stick to the few functions that the experimenters had explained. They were sometimes confused when they invoked an unexpected function with an unintentional gesture.

claim: Multi-mode interfaces without an explicit persistent mode indicator cause elderly users to lose track of the current mode; avoid modes where possible or show large persistent mode indicators.
quote: The participants frequently lost track of their current mode, especially when another mode had a similar look-and-feel.
notes: Guideline: 'Applications should avoid multi-mode interfaces as much as possible... The indicators of mode changes should be persistent and large.'

claim: Slow or heavy taps by elderly users get misrecognized as hold/long-press or drag — touch interfaces for seniors need tolerant tap detection and visible feedback not obscured by the finger.
quote: an overly slow tap can be recognized as a "hold" operation by many applications. Second, exerting more pressure on the screen during a slow motion can cause the finger to draw a random path, which is then recognized as a drag

claim: Icon-only interfaces fail older adults: in a controlled study, participants correctly interpreted only 45% of icons alone vs 78% for icon+label and 79% for label-only — a text label nearly doubles interpretability.
notes: Table 2, icon-only vs icon+label vs label-only. Always pair icons with text labels.

claim: Older adults (65+) correctly interpreted only 60% of existing mobile-device icons vs 75% for younger adults — a large effect size — and only 39% of abstract, semantically-far icons.
quote: Interpretation 75% (1.9%) 60% (1.9%)
notes: N=36; worst condition (abstract+far) for 65+ = 39% interpretation (Table 3).

claim: Icon traits that most help older adults: semantically close meaning (depicted object obviously maps to function), familiarity, concreteness (real-world objects), and text labels.
quote: particular icon characteristics – semantically close meaning (i.e. natural, close link between depicted objects and associated function), familiar, labelled and concrete (i.e. those depicting real-world objects) – improved icon usability for them

claim: Only 33% of older adults prefer learning by trial-and-error vs 86% of younger adults; seniors fear 'messing up' the device or incurring unwanted charges, so novice-first interfaces must be error-proof, undoable, and offer guided step-by-step help.
quote: 86%, a vast majority, of younger respondents chose trial-and-error as one of their three preferred learning methods, but only 33% of older adults reported this preference.
notes: Also: 'fear of breaking the device and the possibility of incurring unwanted charges.'

claim: 63% of older adults prefer learning from the instruction manual (vs <36% of younger), but real manuals fail them: poorly written, unfamiliar terminology, and users can't map manual illustrations to the actual screen — embed step-by-step guidance in the product itself.
quote: 63% of older respondents expressed this preference compared to less than 36% of younger respondents

claim: True beginners care about the exact steps to perform a task, not how the software works — onboard with numbered task steps, demonstrations, and practice, not conceptual explanations.
quote: understanding how the software works was much less important than figuring out the exact steps required to perform a task
notes: Older-beginner subgroup of the field study.

claim: Older adults' decreased finger dexterity causes more errors on mobile devices, compounding their avoidance of exploration — error prevention and easy recovery are core requirements, not polish.
quote: older adults are more prone to making errors on mobile devices due to their relatively decreased finger dexterity

claim: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 requires ≥4.5:1 text contrast (≥3:1 for large-scale text: ≥18pt regular or ≥14pt bold); the ratio exists specifically to compensate for age-related contrast-sensitivity loss, and ~20/40 acuity is typical of elders around age 80 — a senior-first product should target the AAA 7:1 level (SC 1.4.6).
quote: 20/40 is commonly reported as typical visual acuity of elders at roughly age 80.
notes: Also verbatim: 'the user with 20/80 visual acuity would require contrast of about 7:1. This ratio is used in Success Criterion 1.4.6.'

claim: Android's accessibility doc restates the same contrast thresholds in sp units: <18sp text (or bold <14sp) needs ≥4.5:1; all other text ≥3:1.
quote: If the text is smaller than 18sp, or if the text is bold and smaller than 14sp, use foreground and background colors that result in a color contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.

claim: Consensus senior-friendly typography (7 checklists analyzed by W3C WAI-AGE, incl. the NIH/NLM 'Making Your Website Senior Friendly' checklist): body text 12-14pt minimum (up to 14pt), sans serif typeface, medium-or-bold weight, left-justified, increased line/letter spacing, no all-caps runs, underlining only for links.
quote: Minimum text size recommendation | 14 pt | 12 to 14 pt (and relative units to allow scaling) | 12 to 14 pt | 12 pt minimum | Headings larger than text | 12 pt minimum | 12 to 14 pt
notes: 12-14pt print ≈ 16-19px/sp at default density; for low-vision seniors larger is safer.

claim: Senior-friendly interaction consensus (W3C WAI-AGE aggregate incl. NIH/NLM): single clicks only (no double-click/double-tap), larger link targets with clickable margins, space between adjacent links, avoid pull-down/fly-out menus, short pages to minimize scrolling, never disable Back.
quote: Single clicks
notes: NIH/NLM 2002 column; Zaphiris & Kurniawan: 'No double clicks'.

claim: W3C COGA guidance for cognitive/aging users: get to features in the minimum number of easy steps; never require memory across steps (working memory may hold only 1-3 items); new icons/interface paradigms are hard to learn.
quote: People with impaired working memory may only be able to hold one to three items in their memory at the same time.
notes: Also: 'I need to get to the feature I need using the minimum number of easy steps.'

claim: Undo beats confirmation for this audience: users who touch the wrong control need to return in one simple step via predictable back/undo, check work and fix mistakes without losing prior steps.
quote: I need to go back to where I was in one simple step, when I touch the wrong control.
notes: Pattern: 'Always let the user return to a previous point... back and undo features without unwanted data loss.'

claim: Consistency is a load-bearing requirement, not a nicety: controls must stay in expected screen positions and use familiar patterns/icons; users with age-related memory decline may need weeks of repetition to learn a new interface.
quote: I need the controls to be consistently positioned on the screen where I expect them to be.
notes: Also: 'This may take a few weeks of repetition and I may not manage to learn it all if I have a condition affecting learning new things.'

claim: Design synthesis for a never-held-a-phone launcher: ≥48dp (≈9mm) touch targets as floor with 8dp+ gaps and ≥8mm effective targets; text labels on every icon; numbered single-path task flows; explicit always-visible current-location/state; undo everywhere; no double-tap, no hidden gestures, no mode-dependence; ≥4.5:1 (aim 7:1) contrast; sans-serif ~12-14pt+ left-justified text.
quote: interactive objects such as buttons, icons, and clickable text should at a minimum be larger than 8 mm
notes: Synthesis across sources 10-19; each component claim is individually sourced in this file.

claim: Only a handful of icons (home, print, magnifying-glass search) have near-universal recognition; all other icons are ambiguous across interfaces, so every icon needs an accompanying text label — especially for novice/senior users who lack learned conventions.
quote: There are a few icons that enjoy mostly universal recognition from users. The icons for home, print, and the magnifying glass for search are such instances. Outside of these examples, most icons continue to be ambiguous to users due to their association with different meanings across various interfaces.
notes: NN/g industry research, general population.

claim: Icon text labels must be visible at all times without user interaction; hover-revealed labels do not work on touch devices, so GranPhone must use permanent labels under/beside icons.
quote: Icon labels should be visible at all times, without any interaction from the user. For navigation icons, labels are particularly critical. Don't rely on hover to reveal text labels: not only does it increase the interaction cost, but it also fails to translate well on touch devices.

claim: For older adults specifically, text labels on icons and buttons help them memorize functions, locations, and navigation paths.
quote: text labels for icons and buttons can also help older adults memorize functions, locations, and navigation paths
notes: Li & Luximon, BIT 2019, literature-review statement citing multiple prior studies.

claim: The hamburger icon fails with seniors: in a 22-participant older-adult study, 11 could not understand the hamburger icon and the side-drawer entry task saw 29% breakdowns plus 29% complete failures — metaphorical/abstract icons must be avoided or always labelled.
quote: 11 participants could not understand the meaning of hamburger icon. 9 participants could not find the entry point of side drawer at first
notes: Numeric finding; also note participants were high-digital-literacy seniors, so novice users likely worse.

claim: Older adults navigate more effectively through visible content than through menus, icons, and buttons; content-oriented navigation design outperformed menu-oriented patterns in understanding, navigation, and interaction for seniors.
quote: overall older adults were able to navigate using contents more effectively than menus and buttons... the content-oriented navigation design performed better in understanding, navigation, and interaction
notes: Supports big labelled content cards over icon toolbars in GranPhone.

claim: Removing clickability signifiers (flat/ghost styling) measurably hurts findability: eyetracking experiment (n=71) showed 22% longer time and 25% more fixations on weak-signifier pages vs strong-signifier ones.
quote: On average participants spent 22% more time (i.e., slower task performance) looking at the pages with weak signifiers... On average, people had 25% more fixations on the pages with weak signifiers.
notes: General web users on desktop; senior effect plausibly larger but untested.

claim: Older adults struggle to distinguish touchable from non-touchable elements: study found seniors 'could not correctly distinguish between the touchable and non-touchable text' and generally have problems 'differentiating which areas could be touched and which could not.'
quote: 3 users could not correctly distinguish between the touchable and non-touchable text
notes: Reinforces need for unambiguous persistent tappability signifiers.

claim: Elevation/shadow alone does NOT signal tappability to seniors: participants seldom noticed or tapped a floating action button despite its shadow cue, plausibly because declined visual perception impairs reading 3D depth cues; prior studies found older adults prefer raised buttons with visual highlighting and immediate feedback.
quote: Participants reported that they seldom noticed or tapped this button though the floating action button provides an obvious visual cue through the use of shadows. The reason may lie at the decreased visual perception influenced older adults' ability to understand the depth cues of 3D shapes.
notes: Author's causal explanation is hedged in the paper itself; the behavioral finding (FAB unnoticed) is direct. Implication: use filled colored buttons + labels, not just elevation.

claim: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires icons and UI-component visuals needed to understand content/identify controls to have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors — this is the hard floor for GranPhone icon strokes and button boundaries.
quote: The visual presentation of the following have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s): User Interface Components: Visual information required to identify user interface components and states... Graphical Objects: Parts of graphics required to understand the content
notes: Web standard, but standard practice applies it to native apps too.

claim: Thin-line icon strokes lose effective contrast through anti-aliasing on screen, so for low-vision users filled or thick-stroke pictograms are safer than thin outlined icons.
quote: Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin lines and shapes of non-text elements may be rendered with reduced contrast.
notes: Inference from the WCAG warning about thin lines; combined with 3:1 requirement, thin-outlined icon families are risky on cheap 2017-era screens.

claim: Color must never be the only signal: WCAG 1.4.1 forbids using color alone to indicate an action, and icons/symbols should differ by shape as well as color — accept/reject call buttons need distinct glyph shapes and positions in addition to green/red.
quote: Icons and symbols should differ by shape as well as by color.

claim: The green=good/red=bad convention is strong but not colorblind-safe: red-green colorblind users cannot reliably distinguish pure red vs pure green; recommended fixes are adding a redundant non-color cue and/or shifting hues (reddish-orange vs bluish-green) while keeping the cultural semantics.
quote: Users with red-green color blindness have trouble distinguishing red and green... Avoid pure red and green in this situation; a reddish-orange and a bluish-green are distinguishable by color blind users, while still conveying the cultural 'good' and 'bad' meanings to users with normal color vision.
notes: Directly applicable to accept/reject call buttons.

claim: Colorblind users still understand red/green symbolism and designers should retain meaningful colors rather than strip them: interviews with red-green-deficient users found 'color blind people still understand color symbolism'; recommendations — keep meaningful colors, be consistent, allow customization.
quote: Interfaces should retain meaningful colors, consistency is critical, and customization is ideal.
notes: Honors thesis, n=4 interviews — directional only. Conclusion: keep green/red phone conventions AND redundant shape/label/position cues.

claim: Tappability guidance for flat/modern UIs: buttons should 'vaguely look like physical buttons', avoid ghost buttons (thin outline, no fill), never style interactive and static elements identically, reserve a consistent treatment for clickable items, and pair icons with label text.
quote: Make sure your buttons at least vaguely look like physical buttons. Avoid ghost buttons — text with a thin rectangular outline... With few exceptions, these icons should be paired with label text.
notes: Maps to Material filled/tonal buttons rather than outlined/text buttons for seniors.

claim: Voice input is NOT effortless for seniors: in a study of 18 adults 74+, most follow-up reactions were unfavorable — participants kept forgetting the wake word and 'struggled to compose a concise command sentence,' speaking long unstructured sentences that the assistant failed on.
quote: many participants kept forgetting to start a command with a wake word or confused the wake word with other similar words... many participants struggled to compose a concise command sentence for a task. They often spoke lengthy, unstructured, and descriptive sentences
notes: Smart-speaker context; implies GranPhone voice features need forgiving input (push-to-talk, no wake word, confirmation prompts) or voice as output only.

claim: First impressions of voice interaction among seniors were positive — speech was perceived as simple, efficient, convenient — so voice/TTS is worth offering, but it must tolerate mistakes and teach its own operation; a tutorial is only a stopgap since 'a well-designed user interface must be intuitive enough for novice users without needing any manuals or instruction.'
quote: a well-designed user interface must be intuitive enough for novice users without needing any manuals or instruction
notes: Design implications: help users understand how the assistant works, incorporate mistakes/common interaction patterns into design.

claim: Hearing loss is a common barrier to voice/audio interfaces for older adults — TTS output in senior apps should support slow rate, high volume, replay, and always have a visual fallback.
quote: hearing loss imposes a significant challenge to the use of voice assistants for many of them
notes: Inference: paper discusses hearing loss re: voice assistants; the TTS-design recommendations are my extrapolation.

claim: Icon style guidance for seniors: use simple, meaningful, and distinctive icons that avoid look-alike neighbors — older adults struggle to distinguish similar-appearing icons and buttons.
quote: designers should use simple, meaningful and distinctive icons to promote users' recognition and comprehension of assisted navigation buttons

claim: Icons should be simple and schematic — minimal detail, basic object characteristics — since intricate detail is hard to distinguish at small sizes; apply the 5-second rule (if you can't think of an obvious icon in 5s, no icon will communicate it).
quote: Keep the design simple and schematic. Reduce the amount of graphic details by focusing on the basic characteristics of the object rather than creating a highly realistic image in order to speed up recognition. (Intricate details are difficult to distinguish at smaller sizes.)

claim: Smartphone icons in the wild are not designed around seniors' actual needs — a Japanese survey of seniors measured icon intelligibility specifically because older users are 'expected to have the same ability as the youngers' despite mismatched design.
quote: older people are usually expected to have the same ability as the youngers to use smartphones with too many applications, which are obviously not based on the practical needs of the senior
notes: English abstract only; full text Japanese. Weak but corroborating.

claim: Material 3 defines ~45 color roles (primary/on-primary/container pairs, secondary, tertiary, error, surface + 5 surface-container roles, inverse roles, outline, scrim, shadow) that map to Material Components and are used identically whether the scheme is static baseline or dynamic.
quote: You'll use these color roles whether you're using the static baseline scheme or dynamic color.
notes: Diagram caption lists 'all 45 color roles'. Baseline is the default static scheme.

claim: M3 color roles are engineered to guarantee accessible pairings: correctly paired roles deliver a minimum 3:1 contrast; mis-pairing roles can break contrast especially under user-controlled contrast adjustments in dynamic color.
quote: These color pairs provide an accessible minimum 3:1 contrast.

claim: In M3 the error role is intentionally static: it does not change in dynamic color schemes (it still adapts to light/dark theme). Useful precedent for keeping semantic colors (e.g., red hang-up button) fixed in a redesign.
quote: Error is an example of a static color (it doesn't change even in dynamic color schemes). Error color roles are made static by default with any dynamic color scheme.

claim: M3 background/navigation convention: use 'surface' for content background and 'surface container' for navigation areas; text/icons use 'on surface'/'on surface variant'; 'outline' is for important boundaries (text fields) while 'outline variant' is for decorative dividers.
quote: The most common combination of surface roles uses surface for a background area and surface container for a navigation area.

claim: M3 type scale = 15 baseline + 15 emphasized styles spanning Display Large to Label Small, each addressable via tokens (md.sys.typescale.*); emphasized styles (M3 Expressive update) are for selection/primary actions/headlines and are NOT used by components by default.
quote: Material 3 has one type scale containing two sets of type styles: 15 baseline and 15 emphasized. Both of these style sets follow the same scale from Display Large to Label Small.
notes: 'No single product will use all the styles.'

claim: M3 dynamic color has two sources: user-generated (device wallpaper) and content-based (in-app imagery); both produce accessible schemes. On Android, wallpaper-based dynamic color requires API 31+ (Android 12).
quote: There are two ways your product can get a source color: 1. User-generated color from a user's wallpaper 2. Content-based color from in-app content like a music album or book cover.
notes: API-31 requirement corroborated by MDC Color.md: framework dynamic colors 'Starting from Android S'.

claim: M3 requires UIs to support text scaling to a minimum of 200%; when text is resized, text and line height scale proportionally while component padding and inter-element spacing stay at 1x.
quote: UIs should support a minimum text increase of 200%.

claim: M3 prescribed techniques for large text: increase container size, reflow layout (e.g., stack buttons vertically instead of side-by-side at 2x), enable single-direction scrolling (prefer vertical), and use touch-and-hold tooltips for enlarged labels in space-constrained bars (app bars, nav bars, rails, tabs).
quote: Avoid common text resizing issues by increasing container size, reflowing layout, enabling scrolling, and adding tooltips.

claim: M3 button accessibility: enabled buttons need 3:1 contrast vs background (container for elevated/filled/tonal, label text for outlined/text styles); Android button labels should fit within two lines at 200% text size, else provide an alternate way to reach full content; accessibility label must match visible label.
quote: On Android, button labels should be kept concise enough to fit within two lines after the text size is increased to 200%.

claim: M3 reduced-motion guidance: when the platform's reduced-animation setting is on, transitions should use subtle fades instead of sliding/scaling and disable decorative effects (parallax, shape morphing); avoid jump cuts.
quote: If that setting is on, transitions should: Use subtle fades instead of intense sliding or scaling animations; Disable decorative effects like parallax or shape morphing.

claim: M3 Expressive (May 2025) introduced a spring-based motion physics system replacing the easing/duration system; on Jetpack Compose 21 Material components use it by default, while on Android Views (MDC-Android) it is 'Available. Not added to components' — Expressive motion is effectively Compose-first.
quote: On Jetpack Compose, 21 Material components use the motion physics system by default. Android Views (MDC-Android) support is coming soon.

claim: MDC-Android (com.google.android.material, the Views-based Material library) is officially in MAINTENANCE MODE as of Google I/O 2026: no more feature releases; Google is 'all-in' on Compose and recommends migrating Views projects to Compose for the latest Material/Android updates.
quote: This means that the Views-based Material Components for Android library (MDC-Android) is now in maintenance mode.

claim: Google's platform-level position (May 2026): all android.widget View components are in maintenance mode — not deprecated, critical bug fixes continue, but no new features; 'all Android UI should be built with Compose'.
quote: We now consider the View components that Compose replaces (components in the android.widget package) to be in maintenance mode. We have no plans to deprecate or remove View components and will continue to support them with critical bug fixes, but they will receive no new features.

claim: Latest MDC-Android release is 1.14.0 (Google Maven metadata, lastUpdated 2026-05-13); it requires minSdkVersion 23+ and compileSdk 36.1+, AGP 8.13, Android Studio Narwhal 3 FD 2025.1.3. Material3Expressive themes exist only in 1.14.0+.
quote: Required `minSdkVersion` is now 23 or higher, for Material and AndroidX.
notes: minSdk bumped at 1.14.0-alpha09 (commit cd3f114).

claim: MDC-Android 1.13.0 is the last release line supporting minSdkVersion 21; Material3 (non-Expressive) themes require >=1.5.0, so on minSdk 21 the practical ceiling is MDC 1.13.0 with full M3 themes/components (incl. new toolbars, loading indicator, split button, button group) but without M3 Expressive styles.
quote: Required `minSdkVersion` is now 21 or higher, for Material and AndroidX.
notes: 1.13.0 states minSdk 21; 1.14.0 states minSdk 23 — 'last version for API 21' inferred from release ordering.

claim: A minSdk-21 app CAN still use modern M3 theming in Views via MDC 1.13.0; alternatively, since the Android 8 Huawei target hardware is API 26, raising minSdk to 23 unlocks MDC 1.14.0 incl. Expressive themes — only Android 5.x/6.0 (API 21-22) devices would be excluded.
quote: In order to use the new Material3Expressive themes and component styles, you should depend on version 1.14.0 or later.
notes: Decision hinge: does fleet include real API 21/22 devices? Android 6.0 = API 23.

claim: With MDC-Android, dynamic color degrades gracefully: DynamicColors.applyToActivitiesIfAvailable/applyToActivityIfAvailable only applies the dynamic theme overlay on Android S+ (API 31); below that the app keeps its baseline M3 scheme automatically — no separate fallback theme needed.
quote: If the app is running on Android S+, dynamic colors will be applied to the activity.
notes: Baseline palette tokens defined for every role (Primary=primary40) vs dynamic 31-33 (system_accent1_*) and 34+ (system_*_light).

claim: Jetpack Compose runs on API 21+ ('select API level 21 or higher' as the minimum), but Compose UI code must be written in Kotlin — a Java-only codebase cannot write composables without adding Kotlin sources.
quote: In the Language drop-down menu, Kotlin is the only available option because Jetpack Compose works only with classes written in Kotlin.
notes: minSdk 21 also on hardware-accel doc: 'Jetpack Compose requires a minimum of API level 21.'

claim: Compose accessibility is strong out of the box: Material composables enforce 48dp minimum touch target internally when actionable; undersized clickable composables still get expanded touch areas automatically; semantics/contentDescription, traversal order, user-scalable content, and a11y testing APIs are first-class.
quote: When the size of a clickable composable is smaller than the minimum touch target size, Compose still increases the touch target size. It does so by expanding the touch target size outside of the boundaries of the composable.

claim: Android accessibility baseline (applies to Views and Compose): every interactive element needs >=48x48dp touch target ('larger is even better'); text contrast >=4.5:1 for text under 18sp (or bold under 14sp), >=3:1 otherwise.
quote: For touch interfaces, we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better.

claim: Compose on weak hardware requires discipline: debug builds carry a real performance cost (release mode + R8 required to judge perf), and Baseline Profiles should be used to precompile critical journeys (Compose ships a default profile).
quote: Debug mode is useful for spotting many problems, but it imposes a performance cost and can make it hard to spot other issues.
notes: Google claims 'out of the box, Compose offers native performance' (Compose-first blog, L2) under release-build conditions.

claim: Assessment for GranPhone: Compose is technically viable on minSdk 21 and Android 8 hardware, but it forces Kotlin, needs release-build tuning (R8 + Baseline Profiles) to perform on 2017 devices, and Views+MDC now sits in maintenance mode too — so 'safe' = Views with MDC 1.13.0 (or 1.14.0 if minSdk raised to 23); 'future-proof' = Compose despite migration cost.
quote: There are no more planned feature releases for Views, so all projects using the Views library should begin or continue migrating to Compose to get the latest Material Design and Android platform updates.
notes: Synthesis of facts 12-21; only Compose receives new components/motion/a11y work going forward.

claim: Edge-to-edge degrades gracefully on old Android: enforced only when targetSdk>=35 on Android 15+ devices; on older versions (incl. Android 8) it is opt-in via androidx.core WindowCompat.enableEdgeToEdge() in Activity.onCreate — an app can simply not call it and system bars stay conventionally opaque.
quote: To enable edge-to-edge on previous Android versions, manually call enableEdgeToEdge in onCreate of your Activity.
notes: Default e2e: transparent bars; 3-button nav gets translucent scrim; icon colors auto-adjust to light/dark theme.

claim: If edge-to-edge is enabled anywhere, overlaps must be fixed with WindowInsetsCompat: pad/margin tappable views by systemBars() insets (OR displayCutout() for lists), and set clipToPadding on RecyclerViews so content scrolls behind the bars.
quote: System bars insets are the most commonly used type of insets. They represent the area where the system UI displays in the Z-axis above your app.

claim: iOS Assistive Access is a distinct iOS mode designed for cognitive disabilities: bigger onscreen items, more focused features, easier navigation — Apple's stated design principles.
quote: Assistive Access is a distinctive iOS experience that makes it easier for people with cognitive disabilities to use iPhone independently. ... onscreen items are bigger, features are more focused, and it's easier to navigate and understand what actions are possible.

claim: Assistive Access offers two home-screen layouts chosen at setup: Grid (bigger items, icon/image-emphasized) and Rows (readable list).
quote: Rows: Onscreen items are arranged in an easily readable list. Grid: Onscreen items are bigger and arranged in a grid that emphasizes images and icons.
notes: Two layout archetypes: icon-grid vs list — user/caretaker picks per preference for visuals vs text.

claim: Assistive Access uses a 'trusted supporter' model: a family member or caregiver performs setup and personalization, including account/passcode access, entirely outside the mode.
quote: Assistive Access may be easiest to set up with the assistance of a trusted supporter—a family member or caregiver who knows the person who will be using iPhone and can help them choose the apps and features best suited to their needs.

claim: Assistive Access is gated by its own passcode (separate from device passcode) used to enter, exit, and change settings; exit is triple-click side/Home button + passcode. A recovery Apple Account can be set so a caretaker can reset it remotely.
quote: Set an Assistive Access passcode, which is used to enter or exit Assistive Access and change Assistive Access settings. ... To exit Assistive Access at any time, triple-click the side button (on an iPhone with Face ID) or the Home button (on other iPhone models), tap Exit Assistive Access, then enter the Assistive Access passcode.
notes: Caretaker-lock pattern: user inside mode cannot escape or reconfigure without passcode.

claim: In Assistive Access, Phone and FaceTime are merged into a single 'Calls' app; the supporter whitelists who can call/be called (anyone, all contacts, or favorites only) and favorites appear on the app's first screen.
quote: the Phone and FaceTime apps are combined into a single Calls app ... Favorite contacts are shown on the first screen when the Calls app is opened in Assistive Access.
notes: Patterns: merge overlapping apps into one task-named app; favorites-first screen; inbound+outbound contact whitelisting.

claim: Assistive Access requires confirmation for committal actions: ending a call and declining a call each require tapping the button twice to confirm; a persistent Back button exists on every screen.
quote: To hang up, tap End Call, then tap End Call again to confirm. ... On any screen in Assistive Access, the person using Assistive Access can always tap Back to return to the previous screen.

claim: Assistive Access suppresses runtime permission pop-ups — the supporter pre-sets app permissions during setup; Settings app, notifications, status icons (network, Bluetooth, location, Airplane Mode) are removed entirely inside the mode.
quote: To minimize pop-ups while using iPhone, apps won't ask for permission to access information such as location, photos, and contacts. ... there is no Settings app or notifications in Assistive Access ... Certain app privacy information, status icons, and symbols aren't available in Assistive Access, including those that indicate network availability, Airplane Mode, Focus, or Bluetooth
notes: Removes-vs-keeps list: no pop-ups, no Settings, no notifications, no status bar indicators.

claim: Assistive Access Messages supports an emoji-only keyboard and video-selfie messages as visual alternatives to text; messages can be read aloud via Tap to Hear.
quote: messages can be sent with an emoji-only keyboard or as a video selfie
notes: Visual-first communication alternatives; Tap-to-hear detail from Messages page (see open angles).

claim: Third-party apps can be added to Assistive Access only in their original form — only Apple's optimized apps (Calls, Camera, Messages, Music, Photos, Magnifier, TV) get the simplified treatment; App Store is not accessible inside the mode.
quote: You can add apps that have been optimized for Assistive Access, and most other iOS apps in their original design.
notes: App Store exclusion documented on the add/remove-apps page; simplification only works where Apple redesigned the app.

claim: Samsung Easy Mode is a display-level toggle (Settings > Display > Easy mode) that enlarges on-screen items, provides a high-contrast keyboard, and increases touch-and-hold delay to prevent accidental touches — all other apps/settings remain intact.
quote: It will enlarge the on-screen items, provide a high contrast keyboard, and help prevent accidental touches when tapping. From Settings, tap Display, and then tap Easy mode.
notes: Contrast with Apple: same user, reversible switch, no separate environment or passcode.

claim: Samsung Easy Mode restructures the launcher into dedicated panels: left home screen holds a Magnifier widget, another panel is a Contacts page where favorite contacts can be pinned to the home screen for quick calling.
quote: Swipe to the left your Home Screen ... Tap on Magnifier ... Swipe across the Home Screen to view your Contacts page ... Select Create Contact or Add existing contact
notes: Pattern: dedicate a home-screen page to favorite contacts (call-by-face) and another to a magnifier tool.

claim: Xiaomi Lite mode is a home-screen style option (Settings > Home screen > Home screen > Lite mode) intended to make the phone 'easier to view, understand and operate'; a persistent 'Lite mode is on' entry in Settings provides an always-visible exit path.
quote: The Xiaomi smartphone supports the Lite mode, making the phone easier to view, understand and operate. ... To turn off this function, please go to [Settings] and tap on [Lite mode is on]. Then tap [Turn off Lite mode].
notes: Pattern: sticky discoverable exit affordance inside Settings while mode is active.

claim: Huawei EMUI Simple Mode enlarges home-screen icons and fonts, simplifies layout, and automatically maximizes volume — uniquely addressing hearing as well as vision; long-press icon editing is retained and exit is a one-tap 'Exit Simple mode' in Settings.
quote: Simple mode adopts a more concise layout for easy navigation, enlarges icons and fonts for the home screen, and maximizes the volume. ... Touch and hold any icon to drag it to the desired location or uninstall it if it is not a mandatory app.
notes: Auto max volume = multi-sensory accommodation; keeps layout editable rather than locked.

claim: Stock Android offers no unified senior mode but granular accessibility levers: font size up to 200%, independent display-size slider, bold text, outline/high-contrast text, color correction (4 profiles + intensity), color inversion, remove animations, and extra dim — surfaced in Quick Settings and the first-boot setup wizard.
quote: You can adjust font size up to 200%. ... You can also find accessibility settings in quick settings ... These settings can also be set up from the start in the setup wizard.
notes: A senior launcher on Android should pre-compose these levers rather than expecting users to find them.

claim: Pattern: caretaker-configured contact whitelists (favorites-first, restrict inbound/outbound) appear in Apple's model; Samsung/Xiaomi/Huawei modes instead pin contacts to home screens without restricting who can call.
quote: Allow the person using Assistive Access to receive calls from anyone, from all contacts in the Contacts app, or from favorite contacts only
notes: Synthesis across Apple vs Android OEM modes; Android modes are cosmetic, Apple's is a gated environment.

claim: Pattern: Android OEM simple modes (Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei) are single-toggle, user-reversible display changes that keep all apps and settings reachable; only Apple's Assistive Access is a locked, passcode-gated environment with administration moved entirely outside the mode.
quote: From Settings, tap Display, and then tap Easy mode. Tap the switch to turn it on.
notes: Two architectures: cosmetic launcher swap vs separate accessibility environment. BaldPhone-style products target the former or a launcher-app version of the latter.

claim: Pattern: accidental-touch mitigation via timing — Samsung Easy Mode lengthens the touch-and-hold recognition delay so icons aren't moved/triggered by unsteady taps.
quote: help prevent accidental touches when tapping
notes: Configurable long-press delay detail also confirmed in Samsung DE/JP Easy Mode pages (not separately noted).

claim: Pattern: confirmation-everything vs prevention — Apple re-asks on every committal action inside the mode; Samsung prevents the accidental input up front via touch timing. Both address tremor/unsteady touch.
quote: tap End Call, then tap End Call again to confirm
notes: Design trade-off: double-confirm adds friction; longer-press adds latency. Worth testing both.

claim: Pattern: keep emergency paths unconditional — emergency calling in Assistive Access works even when the phone is locked via hardware-button triple-click, independent of contact whitelists.
quote: You can make an emergency call while Assistive Access is active, even if iPhone is locked.
notes: Any senior-mode design must never let simplification gating block emergency calls.

claim: Pattern: visual-over-text defaults — Apple's grid layout emphasizes images/icons, contacts are shown as photo+name, and emoji-keyboard/video messages replace typing; the alternative 'Rows' list exists for users who prefer text.
quote: Assistive Access offers ways for people to navigate iPhone and communicate using visuals rather than text.
